clue.text: Mexican snack stack — hot, without any wrappers

indicators.note: A wrapper is what goes round the outside, so each word named here loses the letter at either end before it joins the build.

parts.note: peel the S and the K off stack and TAC is what is left
hot loses its H and its T, leaving one middle letter

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is pure street food, and that is the misdirection: 'stack' and 'hot' are being treated as spellings on a page, not as things to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: Mexican snack -> TACO: the folded tortilla is the standard example, so a general phrase is pointing at one particular item of Mexican street food.

clue.text: Forgetfulness leads to open bolts — then four being eaten by wild cat

indicators.note: The lead of a word is the letter at its front, so what follows contributes only its initials.

parts.note: the front letter of each of the two words

indicators.note: Whatever is eaten ends up inside the eater, so one chunk is swallowed whole by the creature named next.

parts.note: the wild cat is a lion, and it is the one doing the swallowing
four in Roman numerals is IV, and it goes in after the lion's opening L

explanation.walkthrough: 'Forgetfulness leads to open bolts' reads as a sentence about mislaying things, which is what hides the instruction: 'leads' is asking for initials, not for consequences.
explanation.definitionFit: Forgetfulness -> OBLIVION: the total version of it, the state of having forgotten everything, as in drinking yourself into it.

clue.text: Still one imagined terrifying creature from the Himalayas

definitions.text: imagined terrifying creature from the Himalayas

parts.note: still and yet both mean 'even now'
one as a Roman numeral is I

explanation.walkthrough: Two of the smallest words in the language do all the work, and everything after them is definition — the mountains are described, never named.
explanation.definitionFit: imagined terrifying creature from the Himalayas -> YETI: the abominable snowman of Himalayan legend, reported in footprints and photographs and never in the flesh.

clue.text: Sister Edna eloped, heading north, carrying flowering plant

indicators.note: North is up the page and this entry is written downwards, so the run of letters is read against the way it is printed.
A carrier holds its load inside itself, so these words are concealing a passenger rather than defining one.

parts.note: sisteR EDNA ELOped holds the unbroken run REDNAELO, and read the other way it is the answer

explanation.walkthrough: The sister and the elopement are pure story. Nothing needs solving: the letters simply run on through three words, and a down entry read upwards is what 'heading north' asks for.
explanation.definitionFit: flowering plant -> OLEANDER: an evergreen shrub carrying pink or white blooms, poisonous in every part, common round the Mediterranean.

clue.text: In France a supermarket sacking head to become international organisation

indicators.note: The word beside it must be translated before it is spelt out, so the little word arrives in French rather than English.
Sacking someone gets rid of them, and the head of a word is the letter at its front, so the first letter goes.

parts.note: a in French is un
the supermarket is Tesco, and its head T has just been sacked

explanation.walkthrough: Crossword French is worth banking early: UN, LE, EST and their friends turn up constantly, and 'in France' is the usual flag that one of them is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: international organisation -> UNESCO: the United Nations' education, science and culture agency, so the category is being defined by one body inside it.

clue.text: Absolute chaos, upset jewellery — piecing it all together?

indicators.note: Something upset has been knocked out of the arrangement it was sitting in, and letters knocked out of arrangement come back in another order.

parts.note: absolute chaos is A MESS, and those five letters come back in this order
bling is showy jewellery

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is earning its place: the clue describes its own construction, since putting the pieces back together is exactly what it is asking you to do.
explanation.definitionFit: piecing it all together? -> ASSEMBLING: putting parts into a working whole, the flat-pack sense of the verb, and the -ing ending agrees.

clue.text: Floppy elephant with no stuffing for clingy type

parts.note: limp is floppy

indicators.note: Stuffing is what fills the middle of something, so the beast keeps its first and last letters and nothing between them.

parts.note: hollow the elephant out and its outer E and T remain

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface is about shellfish: 'clingy type' does the defining, and the elephant is in the clue only because its two ends spell what is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: clingy type -> LIMPET: the shellfish grips its rock so hard you cannot prise it off, which is why a person who will not let go gets called one.

clue.text: Tax bill came at last — virtually cleared out

indicators.note: Coming at last means coming at the end, so it is the closing letter of each word in front that is wanted.
A cleared-out room keeps its walls and loses its contents, so the word holds on to its first and last letters only.

parts.note: the final letters of bill and of came
clear everything out from between the V and the Y

explanation.walkthrough: Every word here is doing spelling work rather than meaning work — the bill, the arrival and the 'virtually' are all just letters to be trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Tax -> LEVY: money raised by official demand, the same idea named for the act of collecting rather than for the sum collected.

clue.text: Not the first to risk travel at a leisurely pace

indicators.note: Refusing the first of something means starting one along, so the opening letter of the word is left behind.

parts.note: to risk is to GAMBLE, and that word arrives without its opening G

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not the first to risk' sounds like caution about going early, which is the wrong reading entirely: 'first' is counting letters, not people.
explanation.definitionFit: travel at a leisurely pace -> AMBLE: to walk without hurry, the unpressed gait a horse or a Sunday stroller falls into.

clue.text: Rocks falling and getting into dell is ruinous

indicators.note: A ruinous event leaves what it touches in pieces on the ground, and letters left in pieces have to be picked up in some other order.

parts.note: a dell is a small wooded hollow; four letters of the mix
the clue's own and, three more letters
the last two letters of the mix come from is

explanation.walkthrough: Nine letters sit in plain view across three ordinary little words, and the collapsing valley the surface describes is the same picture the answer paints.
explanation.definitionFit: Rocks falling -> LANDSLIDE: a hillside coming down all at once, the single noun for exactly the event those two words describe.

clue.text: Old nip of rum I drink too, without finishing first shots

indicators.note: A nip is the smallest measure anyone pours, so only a single letter is taken from the spirit named next.
Something left unfinished stops before its end, so the closing letter of the word never arrives.

parts.note: O is the standard short form of old
one letter poured out of rum
the clue's own I, taken as the letter
the drink is gin
too is ALSO, stopped one letter short

explanation.walkthrough: Two spirits and neither of them wanted whole: the bar vocabulary is what makes this read as a night out instead of a spelling exercise.
explanation.definitionFit: first shots -> ORIGINALS: photographers call the earliest takes the originals, the versions every later copy is made from.

clue.text: Space put by, but oddly nothing inside

parts.note: printers measure space in ems, an em being the width of a capital M

indicators.note: Counting oddly means keeping the first, third and fifth letters and leaving the even-numbered ones where they lie.

parts.note: the odd letters of put by: P, T and Y

explanation.walkthrough: 'Space' is a printer's term here, which is the hard step; 'put by', meaning saved for later, is in the clue only to be counted through.
explanation.definitionFit: nothing inside -> EMPTY: a box with nothing in it is empty, so the phrase describes the state and the answer is the adjective for it.

clue.text: Turned and ran away, clutching Zippo but dropping case

indicators.note: To clutch something is to hold it tight against you, so what follows goes inside what came before.

parts.note: ran away is fled, and it opens up to take a passenger

indicators.note: A case is the shell a thing travels in, so the letter at each end of the lighter falls away and the middle survives.

parts.note: the lighter drops its outer Z and O

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dropping case' is a neat double sense: a Zippo really has a case, and in crosswords dropping the case means losing the letters at both ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Turned -> FLIPPED: turned over, the way a pancake or a switch is flipped, and both words equally cover a sudden loss of temper.

clue.text: Scourge of old?

indicators.note: To scourge is to lash and lay waste, and what has been laid waste does not stay in the order it started in.

parts.note: the five letters of 'of old' are the five letters of the answer, in a new order

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, and every one of them is working twice — the clue defines and spells at the same time, which is what makes it an &lit.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the biblical deluge was the great scourge of ancient times, and those same two words supply the letters.

clue.text: Our copter's flying around island territory

indicators.note: Things flying around come down in no particular arrangement, so the letters settle wherever they land.

parts.note: nine letters of the mix; the ’s is only 'is' holding the sentence up
I is the map abbreviation for island

explanation.walkthrough: 'Island' is doing two jobs at once — one letter of the mix, and the picture the answer turns out to fit. The (6,4) tells you how big the mix has to be.
explanation.definitionFit: territory -> PUERTO RICO: not a US state but an unincorporated territory, which is the exact legal word for what it is.

clue.text: Part in test regarding the way planets travel

indicators.note: The little word says one piece sits within another rather than beside it.

parts.note: an oral is a test you sit by speaking; it splits after two letters
a part of something is a bit of it

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue rests on one piece of vocabulary: an oral is a spoken examination, so 'test' is a noun to be swapped, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: regarding the way planets travel -> ORBITAL: of an orbit, so the adjective covers anything belonging to a circling path, a motorway included.

clue.text: Inadvertently Rickrolled — but only part of the words!

definitions.note: The words of a song are usually called the lyrics, in the plural; the singular lyric names the same body of writing taken as one thing.

indicators.note: Taking only part of something means reading a stretch of it exactly as it stands, without altering a letter.

parts.note: the run bridges the two words, ending partway into the second

explanation.walkthrough: Being Rickrolled is being sent that song when you were expecting something else, so the surface jokes about quoting it accidentally — and it really is quoted here.
explanation.definitionFit: the words -> LYRIC: the sung text of a song as against its tune, the sense in which a writer is credited with the lyric.

clue.text: Snow leopard jumps without limits

indicators.note: The limits of a written word are the letters at its two ends, and removing them leaves the middle standing by itself.

parts.note: jumps is BOUNCES, and stripping the B and the S leaves these five

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface hints at letters: 'without limits' reads as unbounded enthusiasm, and 'jumps' has to be turned into a longer word before anything can be taken from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Snow leopard -> OUNCE: ounce is the old name for that cat, a sense which now survives mainly in crosswords and in natural history writing.

clue.text: Harsh fightback

indicators.note: The word ends in the direction of travel, and something coming back arrives the other way round from how it set off.

parts.note: the fight buried in the word is a war; the -back on the end is the instruction, not fodder

explanation.walkthrough: One word of the clue is carrying two jobs: on the surface 'fightback' is a single noun, and underneath it is a piece of fodder with its instruction stuck to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Harsh -> RAW: a raw wind or a raw deal is a harsh one, the sense of unsoftened rather than the uncooked one.

clue.text: An odd owl disturbed some trees

indicators.note: Disturbing something knocks it out of the settled arrangement it was in, which is what happens to these eight letters.

parts.note: the eight letters of AN ODD OWL, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd' looks like the standard instruction to take alternate letters and is really part of the material — a reliable Guardian trap worth learning.
explanation.definitionFit: some trees -> WOODLAND: land under trees taken collectively, so a plural picture is defined by the mass noun that covers it.

clue.text: Central pub evacuated earlier

parts.note: a pub is an inn

indicators.note: An evacuated building has everybody out of the middle of it, so the word keeps only the letters at its two ends.

parts.note: clear out earlier and the E and R at its ends survive

explanation.walkthrough: Five letters, two of them from a word contributing no meaning at all: 'earlier' is in the clue purely so that it can be hollowed.
explanation.definitionFit: Central -> INNER: the inner ring or the inner circle is the one nearest the middle, so both words name the same position.

clue.text: Safe 'n' sound? Two extinct every second!

indicators.note: Taking every second letter means stepping through the words two at a time and writing down only the ones you land on.

parts.note: step through N-S-O-U-N-D-T-W-O-E-X-T-I-N-C-T taking the first, third, fifth and so on

explanation.walkthrough: 'Safe 'n' sound' is a set phrase and that is the trap: the apostrophe-n is not standing in for 'and', it is the first letter you count from.
explanation.definitionFit: Safe -> NON-TOXIC: safe in the narrow sense of not poisonous, which is what a paint tin or a child's toy label means by the word.

clue.text: Be taken the wrong way during rendezvous, creating arguments

indicators.note: Taking a word the wrong way round means writing its letters from the far end back to the start.
What happens during an event happens inside it, so this piece is placed within the other.

parts.note: rendezvous are dates, and the word opens after its D
the clue's own Be, turned round

explanation.walkthrough: 'Be taken the wrong way' is what happens to a remark in a row, so the instruction is hiding inside a description of the very thing the answer names.
explanation.definitionFit: arguments -> DEBATES: formal ones, run to rules with two sides and a motion, rather than the shouting the definition can also cover.

clue.text: Welsh city's non-governmental organisation gathered by bar

indicators.note: To gather something up is to take it into your arms, so the piece named next closes right around it.

parts.note: the bar is taken as it stands and splits after two letters
NGO is the standard abbreviation, used by every news bulletin

explanation.walkthrough: An abbreviation from the news does the work here; the aid-agency-and-pub scene on the surface is entirely the setter's invention.
explanation.definitionFit: Welsh city -> BANGOR: the small cathedral city on the Menai Strait in Gwynedd, so the answer is one instance of the category.

clue.text: Flow of vapour engulfing opening of railway

indicators.note: To engulf is to swallow up completely, so the letter that follows disappears inside the word before it.

parts.note: the vapour off a kettle is steam

indicators.note: The opening of a word is the letter it begins with, so nothing but that initial is taken.

parts.note: the first letter of railway, which is also its usual abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: Steam and railways belong together on the surface, and that is what stops you noticing that one is a word to be opened up and the other only a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Flow -> STREAM: a stream of water, traffic or talk is a continuous flow, the noun for anything moving steadily in one direction.

clue.text: Naturally produced grain ruined through company backtracking

indicators.note: A ruined thing has lost the shape it was built in, so its letters come back in a different arrangement.

parts.note: company shortens to CO, which backtracks to OC and then opens around the rest

indicators.note: Going through something means passing inside it, so the jumbled letters end up within the other piece.
To backtrack is to retrace your steps the way you came, so the abbreviation is written from its end to its start.

parts.note: the five letters of grain in a new order

explanation.walkthrough: CO for company is a workhorse abbreviation. Here it is reversed and then split, so its two letters finish at opposite ends of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Naturally produced -> ORGANIC: grown without synthetic chemicals, the supermarket-label sense rather than the chemist's meaning of carbon-based.

clue.text: Pitman's system finally starts to introduce new, easy recording

indicators.note: What comes finally comes at the end, so it is the closing letter of the word in front that is used.
The start of a word is its first letter, so each word in the list that follows gives up only its initial.

parts.note: the last letter of system
the initials of the four words, in the order they come

explanation.walkthrough: Pitman's shorthand is the joke — the clue pretends to be about the system, while the definition is only the man's job.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitman -> MINER: pitman is the old colliery word for a man who works down the pit, so this is a plain regional synonym.

clue.text: Greek character with very loud furry garment

parts.note: mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet
fortissimo is written ff on a score

explanation.walkthrough: The music abbreviations are worth banking: p is soft, f is loud and ff is very loud, and setters clue them by volume every time.
explanation.definitionFit: furry garment -> MUFF: the fur tube a Victorian lady slipped both hands into, worn rather than carried, so it counts as clothing.

clue.text: Devout priest, German, in South American city with us

indicators.note: The word puts one set of letters within another instead of alongside it.

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro, which splits open after its first letter
Eli is the priest who raised Samuel, crosswordland's standard clergyman
G is the usual abbreviation for German
the clue's own us, added at the end

explanation.walkthrough: Eli is worth remembering: three letters, a priest, and very nearly the only one setters ever use. The comma-heavy surface hides a straightforward stack.
explanation.definitionFit: Devout -> RELIGIOUS: seriously observant of a faith, a near synonym, though the answer can also mean merely belonging to a church.

clue.text: Desert old boy, captured by US soldier

indicators.note: A captive is held inside by whoever took them, so this pair of letters sits within the soldier.

parts.note: a GI is an American soldier
OB is the standard short form of old boy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Desert old boy' reads as an instruction to abandon a friend, which is the whole trick: the first word is the definition and has nothing to do with the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Desert -> GOBI: the great cold desert of Mongolia and northern China, so a general word is being defined by one famous instance.

clue.text: Place, place and, finally, place

parts.note: to place something is to sit it somewhere

indicators.note: The word marks the end of the one beside it, so nothing but its closing letter is taken.

parts.note: the final letter of the word place itself

explanation.walkthrough: One word repeated three times over, doing three different jobs — definition, synonym, single letter — and that repetition is the whole of the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Place -> SITE: the spot where something stands or happens, as in a building site or the site of a battle.

clue.text: Commanding Officer had info about who's hunting whom?

indicators.note: Letters sent about are turned loose to settle anywhere, so the order they arrive in is not the order they leave in.

parts.note: a Commanding Officer is the CO
seven more letters of the mix, taken as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: The military surface is a decoy: the officer is only an abbreviation, and 'about' is the shuffle rather than the subject of the intelligence.
explanation.definitionFit: who’s hunting whom? -> FOOD CHAIN: the ranking of what eats what in an ecosystem, so the question names it by the thing it records.

clue.text: Constructed crowns of bronze using intricate latticework techniques

indicators.note: The crown is the top of a thing, and at the top of a written word sits the letter it begins with.

parts.note: the initials of the five words, in the order they come

explanation.walkthrough: Five words of craft vocabulary and only their first letters matter; the latticework is there to keep you thinking about metalwork.
explanation.definitionFit: Constructed -> BUILT: the past participle of build, the everyday word for anything put up out of parts.
